text:
Imperial Brands, the owner of Davidoff cigarettes and Blu vapes, is slashing up to 4,600 jobs in a huge cost-cutting drive, as it uses more AI and other technologies.
The Bristol-based company said this year 2,100 roles would go globally, and it plans a further reduction of between 2,100 and 2,500 jobs by the end of 2030.
Imperial Brands, which has a global workforce of about 25,000 people, has closed its Langenhagen factory in Germany and sold another factory in Taiwan, leading to 700 job losses, and is holding consultations on the planned reductions in several countries. The current cuts affect a small number of jobs in the UK.
Lukas Paravicini, the chief executive, said the cuts were part of a “transformation” of the company, with at least £320m of annual savings targeted by 2030.
“We continue to perform and transform,” he said. “We want to become more agile, more data-led, more consumer facing and more efficient.”
He added: “We’re fusing the organisation with more technologies”, including new software and AI.
As cigarette volumes decline, the group – which is also behind the John Player Special, Golden Virginia and Rizla brands – has been revamping its business, moving towards newer products, including vapes, heated tobacco and oral nicotine.
It faces tax increases in Germany and a ban on the advertising of vaping and nicotine products in the UK from next June. Paravicini shrugged the changes off, saying the company had experienced regulation in other countries, and that Blu vape products were growing at double digits in the UK.
He added: “We support regulation on vapes, it will put more clarity in the market.”
The company’s total revenues fell 1.5% to £31.7bn in the year to 30 September. Profit before tax fell 12.1% to £2.7bn.
Imperial Brands posted tobacco net revenue growth of 1.7% in key markets, as it raised its prices by 5.1%, which offset a 3.4% drop in volumes.
Earlier this year, British American Tobacco said it would cut about a fifth of its 47,000-strong workforce this year, as the cigarette maker looked for ways to push down costs and become more “technology enabled”.
BAT, which is one of the biggest tobacco groups in the world, announced it will cut 5,500 jobs by the end of the year and outsource a further 3,500, affecting a total of 9,000 employees.
